food.text: The Caral or Norte Chico civilization of coastal Peru, dating back to 3500 BCE, is the oldest known civilization in the Americas. It arose on a hyper-arid desert coast, where farming was possible only with irrigation in river valleys or in a few fog oases called lomas.
Andean peoples domesticated a wide variety of crops despite high mountains and hyper-arid desert. Potatoes, peppers, peanuts, manioc and coca all became important worldwide.

Some scholars believe the earliest civilizations on the Peruvian coast relied more on maritime resources than on agriculture while their societies were forming. The sea may have fed the first Andean cities more than the fields did.
Lima butter beans, called pallares in Peru, have been part of Peruvian cuisine for at least 6,000 years. They remain a staple ingredient in Peruvian cooking today.
The Andeans domesticated two animals, the llama and the guinea pig. Guinea pigs were among the animals that Andean peoples raised alongside their crops.
Maize found its way to the Andes from Mexico. It was often the most important crop at lower and intermediate elevations.
Andean farmers cultivated an estimated 70 different plants, almost as many as were cultivated in all of Europe and Asia. Many of these plants are no longer cultivated or are only minor crops today.

The Chinchorro lived on the Pacific coast of northern Chile and southern Peru and relied heavily on the sea for food. Shell middens and chemical analysis of human remains indicate that seafood made up about 90 percent of their diet, supplemented by land animals and plants gathered near river mouths.

In the high Andes, farming was limited by thin soils, cold climate, seasonal rainfall and a scarcity of flat land. Freezing temperatures can occur in every month of the year above 3,000 metres, where many highland civilizations made their homes.

art.text: Around 3600 BCE, builders at Sechin Bajo in Peru made a 2-meter-tall adobe frieze, and a circular plaza followed around 3500 BCE. The frieze shows a man holding something in each hand, interpreted as a ritual knife or a ceremonial cane in one hand and a human head or a shield in the other. The frieze and the plaza are the two oldest examples of monumental architecture discovered so far in the Americas.

The Chinchorro of the Pacific coast of northern Chile and southern Peru began deliberately mummifying their dead by about 5050 BCE. Depending on the period and style, bodies could be dismembered and reconstructed, cut open through incisions, reinforced with wooden poles, reeds and clay, fitted with human-hair wigs and finished with mineral pigments. The tradition lasted about 3,000 years, ending around 1800 BCE.

Cerro Sechín in northern Peru has a stone facade decorated with approximately 300 etched bas-reliefs. They show axe-wielding warrior-priests and dismembered victims: decapitated and mutilated bodies, heads, limbs, skewered eyes, intestines, vertebrae and viscera. The slabs may represent the central Andes' oldest known monumental sculpture.

The Caral–Supe civilization of coastal Peru flourished in the 4th and 2nd millennia BCE and is recognized as the oldest-known civilization in the New World. It was known for its density of large sites with immense architecture, and its main city was Caral.

At Cerro Sechín in northern Peru, megalithic walls carry carved figures in bas-relief that graphically dramatize human sacrifices. Many of the carvings show dismembered victims, with heads, limbs, skewered eyes, intestines, vertebrae and viscera. The site dates to about 1600 BC, and its slabs may be the oldest known monumental sculpture in the central Andes.

Kotosh Religious Tradition ritual buildings were built in the Peruvian highlands between about 3000 and 1800 BCE, before pottery was used. Sites such as Kotosh, La Galgada and Huaricoto are separated by considerable distances, yet their public architecture is remarkably similar.

At Kotosh, the earliest identified cultural period was preceramic, and it was then that the Temple of the Crossed Hands was first built. The image of crossed arms is characteristic of the temple iconography of Kotosh.

At Cerro Sechín, two large murals depicting felines once flanked the central stairway of the temple. Although their upper sections have eroded, the clawed feet are still preserved. This imagery may be an early sign of the Cult of the Feline seen later at Chavín de Huántar.

The Third Building at Sechin Bajo, built between about 1600 and 1200 BCE, is the most monumental of the site's structures. It has both public squares and private areas, and many of its walls are decorated with relief carvings.
The Chavín culture has very distinctive art styles, particularly in effigy pots. A number of these pots were made in feline shapes.
A Chinchorro male mummy bears the earliest tattoo found in the Americas. It is a mustache-like dotted line above his upper lip, dated to about 2300 BC.

Inside the adobe building at Cerro Sechín, the best-preserved decoration depicts two mythological fish, and another figure shows a man bleeding. The article says these depictions closely relate to the sea, rain and human sacrifices. Carvers used bevelled cuts for body contours and shallow incisions for details such as eyelids and lips.

war.text: The high stone walls of Cerro Sechín show reliefs of "warrior-priests" with their mutilated enemies. The complex dates back to 1,500-2,000 BC, and the reliefs belong to its latest construction phase.

One reading of the carvings at Cerro Sechín is that they are battle scenes, made to commemorate a great battle. In this view they show foreign victorious warriors and defeated Casma people. The roughly 300 carved reliefs include axe-wielding warriors alongside decapitated and mutilated victims, with heads, limbs, skewered eyes, intestines, vertebrae and viscera shown.

Yet another theory holds that the Cerro Sechín carvings represent a popular bloody rebellion that was crushed by the ruling elite. If so, the stones would record violence within the community rather than a foreign war. The carvings show decapitated and dismembered victims, with heads, limbs, skewered eyes, intestines and viscera, and one figure of a bleeding man.

Who built Cerro Sechín and what ceremonies took place there are unknown, and little is known about the community tied to the site. It was completed before 2000 BC but stayed in use until about 1500 BC, before the Chavín culture began.

Cerro Sechín was discovered on July 1, 1937, by the Peruvian archaeologists Julio C. Tello and Toribio Mejía Xesspe. Tello believed it was the capital of an entire culture, now known as the Casma/Sechin culture or Sechin complex.

science.text: Caral, in the Supe Valley of Peru, is considered the oldest city in the Americas and one of the oldest in the world. No other site in the Americas as early as Caral has such a diversity of monumental buildings with different ceremonial and administrative functions. It was inhabited from around 2600 BC to 2000 BC.

The Caral–Supe civilization flourished along the Fortaleza, Pativilca and Supe rivers, and large-scale settlement and communal construction are clear from 3100 BCE onward. It arose a millennium after Sumer in Mesopotamia and was contemporaneous with the Egyptian pyramids. It is recognized as the oldest-known civilization in the New World.

The Chinchorro did not reserve elaborate funerary treatment for an elite. They preserved men, women and children from across their communities. Depending on the period and style, bodies could be dismembered and reconstructed, cut open through incisions, reinforced with wooden poles, reeds and clay, fitted with human-hair wigs and finished with mineral pigments.

At Paloma, south of Lima, the people ate large deep-water fish such as cabrilla, as well as anchovies and herring. Many of these are deep-water species, so the villagers must have had good seafaring abilities. Yet no boats have been found at Paloma or at preceramic Peruvian sites in general.

Chinchorro mummification changed over time. The mummies were first a shimmering black produced by manganese, and around 2000 BC they became red. High arsenic concentrations in the environment led to high infant mortality among some of the people, which is discussed as the cause of the development of mummification as a social and emotional way of processing death.

As the Caral–Supe civilization declined around 1800 BCE, extensive canals began appearing farther north. Anthropologist Winifred Creamer notes that people were moving to more fertile ground and taking their knowledge of irrigation with them. The success of irrigation-based agriculture at Caral–Supe may have contributed to its being eclipsed.

Some researchers suggest Cerro Sechín was a laboratory for anatomical studies rather than a monument to war. They point to the explicit exposure of parts of the human body in the carvings, such as organs and bones. Other interpretations are that the carvings show human sacrifices offered to the gods, a battle in which foreign victorious warriors defeated the Casma people, or a popular bloody rebellion crushed by the ruling elite.
The proto-Inca cultures of South America continued at a Stone Age level until around 2000 BCE. Only then did gold, copper, and silver make their entrance.
A Chinchorro male mummy bears the earliest tattoo found in the Americas. He has a mustache-like dotted line tattooed above his upper lip. The tattoo dates to about 2300 BC.

Claims of the earliest quipu, or possible proto-quipu, come from the Late Preceramic site of Caral, dated to about 3000 to 1800 BCE. Quipus are record-keeping devices made from knotted cords. The claim has yet to be thoroughly evaluated.

politics.text: The Norte Chico civilization, also called Caral, was a complex society that included as many as 30 major population centers on the north-central coast of Peru. It is the oldest known civilization in the Americas. It flourished between the 30th century BCE and the 18th century BCE.

Scholars generally acknowledge six cradles of civilization, and the Caral-Supe civilization of coastal Peru is one of the two believed to be the earliest in the Americas. A civilization is defined as a complex society marked by the development of a state, social stratification and urbanization.

Andean civilizations are counted among at least five civilizations that scholars deem "pristine." This means one that developed independently of external influences and is not derived from other civilizations. The Caral or Norte Chico civilization is the oldest known of them in the Americas.

The Norte Chico built public monumental architecture at the city of Caral, dated 2627 to 1977 BCE. The culture emerged in Peru around 3100 BCE, in the same era as the early civilizations of Mesopotamia and Egypt.
From 3100 BC onward, large-scale human settlement and communal construction become clearly apparent in Caral-Supe. This lasted until a period of decline around 1800 BC.

All the cradles of civilization relied on farmers producing a surplus to support centralized government, political leaders and public works. Caral-Supe may be the exception, since it may have depended initially on marine resources instead of agriculture.
The alternative name for the Norte Chico civilization, Caral-Supe, comes from the Sacred City of Caral in the Supe Valley. It is a large and well-studied Norte Chico site.

philosophy.text: Archaeologists use the name Kotosh Religious Tradition for ritual buildings built in the mountain valleys of the Peruvian Andes between about 3000 and 1800 BCE. The sites lie far apart, yet their public architecture is remarkably similar. Kotosh was the first to be discovered.

People came to Chavín de Huántar to attend rituals, consult an oracle, or enter a cult. Construction went through many stages starting before 1200 BC, and the site drew people from across the region to worship together.

Caral was inhabited from about 2600 BC to 2000 BC. No other site in the Americas has been found with such a diversity of monumental buildings serving different ceremonial and administrative functions this early.

Around 3000 BCE, farming communities at La Galgada built small chambers separate from their houses, presumably for ceremonial activities. They put more effort into ceremonial and burial monuments than into their own homes.

Julio C. Tello and Toribio Mejía Xesspe discovered Cerro Sechín on July 1, 1937. Tello thought it was the capital of a whole culture, but who built it, how, and what ceremonies took place there are still unknown.
Near the mouth of the Supe River, the fishing city of Áspero was closely tied to Caral. Remains of human sacrifices have been found there: two children and a newborn.

Excavator Terence Grieder described La Galgada as one of the most important ceremonial and burial areas in a well-populated district, which he called virtually a metropolitan center. At least 11 preceramic settlements grew up along the Tablachaca Canyon around it.

At Sechin Bajo, the Second and Third Buildings date from about 1600 to 1200 BCE. The Third Building had public squares, private areas and walls with relief carvings. Both were oriented toward Cerro Sechin, 2 kilometres away, which suggests cooperation or subordination between the builders of the two sites.

Chavín de Huántar stood at the headwaters of the Marañón River, between the coast and the jungle. This made it ideal for spreading and gathering both ideas and material goods, and it became a place of pan-regional importance.
Archaeologist Ruth Shady highlights cultural links between Caral–Supe and the highland Kotosh Religious Tradition. This suggests ritual ideas moved between the coast and the mountains.
Local Huallaga Quechua speakers named Kotosh, and the word means a heap of stones. It refers to the two stony mounds at the site, which lies about 5 kilometres from modern Huánuco.

culture.text: The Caral or Norte Chico civilization of coastal Peru is the oldest known civilization in the Americas, dating back to 3500 BCE. It flourished between the 30th century BCE and the 18th century BCE.
Scholars count Caral-Supe on the coast of Peru as one of six cradles of civilization. Along with the Olmec civilization of Mexico, it is believed to be one of the two earliest in the Americas.

Andean civilizations are counted among at least five in the world that scholars deem "pristine." That means they developed independently of outside influences and did not derive from other civilizations. The Caral civilization of coastal Peru dates back to 3500 BCE.
Chavín de Huantar was an important ritual centre for the Chavín culture, dating to around 1,500 BCE. The Chavín culture is thought to have been primarily a religious movement.

The Chinchorro lived along the Pacific coast of what is now northern Chile and southern Peru. They built small communities near rivers that crossed the Atacama Desert. Shell middens and chemical analysis of human remains indicate that seafood made up about 90 percent of their diet.

The final style of Chinchorro mummification, the mud-coat, dates from 3000 to 1300 BCE. Artisans no longer removed the organs of the dead. Instead they covered the bodies in a thick coat of mud, sand and a binder such as egg or fish glue, and then cemented the mummies into their graves. The change may have come from exposure to outsiders and their different cultures, or from the association of disease with rotting corpses.

The Chinchorro artificially preserved men, women and children from across their communities rather than restricting elaborate funerary treatment to a social elite. Their mummification tradition continued for about 3,000 years, ending around 1800 BCE.

The Norte Chico civilization included as many as 30 major population centers in what is now north-central coastal Peru. It is also called Caral-Supe, a name derived from the Sacred City of Caral in the Supe Valley.
Complex society in Norte Chico arose a millennium after Sumer in Mesopotamia. It was contemporaneous with the Egyptian pyramids and predated the Mesoamerican Olmec by nearly two millennia.
The Chavín culture apparently began in the Peruvian highlands and then spread outward throughout the country. Scholars think it was primarily a religious movement rather than a conventional state.

Ritual buildings of the Kotosh Religious Tradition were built in Peru's mountain drainages from about 3000 to 1800 BCE. Sites such as Kotosh, La Galgada, Shillacoto and Huaricoto are separated by considerable distances. Even so, their public architecture is remarkably similar.

Malleable clay let Chinchorro morticians mold the colorful appearances of their mummies, and it also covered the foul smell of the desiccating body. Clays and gypsum may also help explain the remarkable preservation, since gypsum acts as a natural desiccant.

Caral-Supe may have depended at first on marine resources, unlike the other cradles of civilization, which all relied on agriculture for sustenance. Farming surpluses supported the other early centers, but the coast of Peru may have followed a different path.

The mud-coat style of Chinchorro mummification no longer removed the organs of the dead. Instead, the bodies were covered in a thick coat of mud, sand and a binder such as egg or fish glue, and the clay also covered the foul smell of the desiccating, rotting corpse. Once completed, the mummies were cemented into their graves. The change in style may have come from exposure to outsiders and their different cultures, or from the association of disease with the rotting corpses.
